provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of jss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list types of soil components, explain the importance of soil to crops, and identify major crop groups.

Introduction:
We have studied soil and crops in JSS 2. Today we will revise what we learned to prepare for new topics.

Content:
Soil is made of sand, silt, clay, organic matter and water. Good soil has these in right balance like the soil in our school farm. Crops are plants grown for food like maize, cassava and yam. Each crop needs specific soil type to grow well. For example, rice needs waterlogged soil while maize needs well-drained soil.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to test soil samples from different areas of the school farm and record their findings.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three components of soil.
2. Why is soil important to crops?
3. Give one example of a crop that needs wet soil.
4. How does soil texture affect crop growth?

Summary:
Soil provides nutrients and support for crops while crops are plants grown for food and other uses.

topics.title: Agricultural extension
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define agricultural extension, list the roles of extension agents, and explain the importance of extension services.

Introduction:
We know farmers need information to improve their farming. Agricultural extension workers help farmers get this information.

Content:
Agricultural extension is the process of helping farmers learn new farming methods. Extension agents are teachers who visit farms like extension officers from the Ministry of Agriculture in your local government. They teach about new crop varieties, better seeds, pest control and how to get better prices at the market. For example, an extension officer might teach farmers how to use organic fertilizer from cow dung instead of expensive chemical fertilizer.

Class activity:
Students will role-play extension agents visiting a farm and teaching improved cassava planting methods.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is agricultural extension?
2. Name two roles of extension agents.
3. Why are extension services important to farmers?
4. How can extension agents help increase farm income?

Summary:
Agricultural extension services help farmers learn and adopt better farming practices to improve productivity and income.

topics.title: Farm records
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list different types of farm records, explain the importance of keeping farm records, and demonstrate how to maintain a simple farm record book.

Introduction:
Good farmers keep records like shopkeepers keep records of their sales and expenses. This helps them know if they are making profit or loss.

Content:
Farm records are documents where farmers write information about their farming activities. Types include farm diary, input records, harvest records, sales records and financial records. For example, a farmer might write in the diary that he planted maize on March 1st and harvested on July 15th. Input records show what was bought like seeds, fertilizer and chemicals. Financial records show money spent and earned. Keeping records helps farmers make better decisions next planting season.

Class activity:
Students will create a simple farm record book for a small vegetable farm and record activities for one week.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three types of farm records.
2. Why is it important to keep farm records?
3. What information should be in a farm diary?
4. How can farm records help improve future farming?

Summary:
Keeping good farm records helps farmers track their activities, expenses and income to make better farming decisions.

topics.title: Crop propagation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between sexual and asexual propagation, list methods of asexual propagation, and demonstrate stem cutting propagation.

Introduction:
Plants can be grown from seeds or from parts of other plants. We will learn these different ways of planting crops.

Content:
Crop propagation is how new plants are grown. Sexual propagation uses seeds from flowers like maize seeds from maize cobs. Asexual propagation uses plant parts like stems, roots or leaves to grow new plants. Methods include stem cuttings, root cuttings, layering and budding. For example, cassava is propagated by planting stem cuttings. Mango trees can be propagated by budding. Asexual propagation produces plants that are exactly like the parent plant while sexual propagation may produce plants with different characteristics.

Class activity:
Students will practice stem cutting propagation using cassava stems or sweet potato vines.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between sexual and asexual propagation?
2. Name two crops propagated by stem cuttings.
3. List three methods of asexual propagation.
4. Why might a farmer choose asexual propagation over sexual propagation?

Summary:
Crop propagation can be done through sexual methods using seeds or asexual methods using plant parts, each with advantages for different crops.

topics.title: Nursery practices
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the importance of nurseries, list requirements for a good nursery, and prepare a simple nursery bed.

Introduction:
Some plants need special care when they are young. Nurseries provide this special care for seedlings before they are planted in the field.

Content:
A nursery is a place where young plants are grown until they are strong enough for transplanting. Requirements include good soil, proper drainage, protection from sun and rain, and regular watering. For example, tomato seedlings need shade from the hot sun and regular watering to grow well. The nursery bed should be raised about 15cm above ground level to prevent waterlogging. Seedlings should be thinned to give them enough space to grow. When seedlings are ready, they are transplanted to the main field.

Class activity:
Students will prepare a small nursery bed for vegetable seedlings like tomatoes or peppers.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a nursery?
2. Name three requirements for a good nursery.
3. Why is proper drainage important in a nursery?
4. What happens if seedlings are not thinned properly?

Summary:
Nurseries provide the right conditions for young plants to grow strong before being transplanted to the main field.

topics.title: Cultural practices
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list different cultural practices, explain the importance of each practice, and demonstrate proper weeding techniques.

Introduction:
After planting crops, farmers must take care of them as they grow. These care activities are called cultural practices.

Content:
Cultural practices are activities done to help crops grow well. Tillage is preparing the soil for planting by plowing and harrowing. Planting is putting seeds or seedlings in the soil. Fertilizer application adds nutrients to the soil. Weeding removes unwanted plants that compete with crops for water and nutrients. For example, in a maize farm, weeding is important because grass like spear grass can take water and nutrients meant for the maize plants. Cultural practices should be done at the right time for best results.

Class activity:
Students will practice weeding techniques in the school farm, identifying and removing common weeds.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are cultural practices?
2. Name three cultural practices.
3. Why is weeding important in crop production?
4. What happens if cultural practices are not done at the right time?

Summary:
Cultural practices like tillage, planting, fertilizing and weeding are essential for healthy crop growth and good harvests.

topics.title: Manures and fertilisers
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between manures and fertilizers, list examples of each, and explain the proper application methods.

Introduction:
Crops need nutrients to grow well. These nutrients can come from natural sources like animal waste or from manufactured products.

Content:
Manures are organic materials from plants and animals that add nutrients to the soil. Examples include cow dung, poultry droppings, compost and farmyard manure. Fertilizers are inorganic materials manufactured in factories that supply specific nutrients to plants. Examples include NPK, urea and sulfate of ammonia. Manures improve soil structure while fertilizers provide quick nutrient supply. For example, a farmer might apply poultry manure to a vegetable garden before planting and add NPK fertilizer when the plants are growing. Manures should be applied two weeks before planting to allow them to decompose properly.

Class activity:
Students will prepare a simple compost heap using farm waste and learn how to apply it to soil.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between manures and fertilizers?
2. Name two examples of organic manures.
3. Why should manures be applied before planting?
4. What nutrients do NPK fertilizers provide?

Summary:
Manures and fertilizers both provide nutrients to crops but differ in source, composition and application methods.

topics.title: Pests of crops
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to classify crop pests, list common pests of major crops, and explain pest control methods.

Introduction:
Pests are organisms that damage crops and reduce yields. We need to identify and control them to protect our crops.

Content:
Crop pests are organisms that harm plants by feeding on them, transmitting diseases or causing damage. They can be insects, birds, rodents, mammals or other animals. Common pests include grasshoppers that eat leaves, birds that eat grains, rats that harvest stored crops, and aphids that suck sap from plants. For example, in a maize farm, birds can destroy the cobs just before harvest. Pest control methods include cultural control like crop rotation, biological control using natural enemies, chemical control using pesticides, and physical control like traps. Regular pest scouting helps detect pests early before they cause serious damage.

Class activity:
Students will go on a pest scouting exercise in the school farm, identifying and recording any pests found.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are crop pests?
2. Name three types of crop pests.
3. How can pests affect crop yield?
4. What is pest scouting and why is it important?

Summary:
Crop pests can cause significant damage but can be controlled through various methods when detected early.

topics.title: Diseases of crops
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between fungal, bacterial and viral diseases, identify common symptoms of crop diseases, and explain disease control measures.

Introduction:
Just like humans, plants can get diseases that affect their growth and productivity. We need to recognize these diseases to control them.

Content:
Crop diseases are caused by fungi, bacteria, viruses or nematodes that attack plants. Fungal diseases like maize streak disease cause spots on leaves. Bacterial diseases like blight cause wilting and rotting. Viral diseases like mosaic cause yellowing and stunting of plants. For example, cassava mosaic disease causes the leaves to become mottled and the plant to produce small roots. Disease control includes using resistant varieties, crop rotation, proper sanitation, and fungicides or bactericides. Early detection is important to prevent spread. Farmers should remove and destroy infected plants to protect healthy ones.

Class activity:
Students will examine crop samples showing different disease symptoms and try to identify the possible causes.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three types of crop disease-causing organisms.
2. What are symptoms of cassava mosaic disease?
3. How can crop rotation help control diseases?
4. Why is early detection of crop diseases important?

Summary:
Crop diseases can be caused by various pathogens and can be controlled through proper management practices when detected early.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer past BECE questions correctly, identify key concepts from the term's work, and demonstrate proper examination techniques.

Introduction:
We have covered many topics this term. Today we will practice answering examination questions to prepare for our BECE.

Content:
We will review important concepts from agricultural extension, farm records, crop propagation, nursery practices, cultural practices, manures and fertilizers, pests and diseases. Students will practice answering multiple-choice, theory and practical questions from past BECE agricultural science papers. We will discuss proper ways to answer questions, read instructions carefully, manage time, and show working where required. For example, when asked to explain the difference between manures and fertilizers, students should give clear, concise points covering source, composition and effect on soil.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past BECE questions and present their answers to the class for discussion.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the role of agricultural extension agents.
2. Differentiate between sexual and asexual propagation.
3. List three requirements for a good nursery.
4. How can crop rotation help control pests and diseases?
5. What is the importance of keeping farm records?

Summary:
Regular practice with past examination questions helps students understand question patterns and improve their performance in the BECE.
